name: Alan Turing
kicker: A founder of computer science · Helped crack Germany’s Enigma code
briefing: Alan Turing was a British mathematician who imagined a simple machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape, an idea that became the basic model of what every computer can do. During World War II he worked at Bletchley Park, where machines he designed, called bombes, helped read Germany’s secret Enigma messages. He also asked whether machines could think, and computer science’s highest honor, the Turing Award, is named for him.
answerHtml: Alan Turing (accept Turing; do not accept “Turing machine” or “Turing test”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: In his 1938 Princeton dissertation, supervised by Alonzo Church, this man introduced “oracle” machines that can answer questions no ordinary machine can. Two years earlier, he and Church had each shown that David Hilbert’s “decision problem” has no general solution.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who imagined a computing machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape.

tossups.p: This man invented a statistical method named for Banbury, the town where its long paper sheets were printed, to help find the daily settings of German navy messages. He led Hut 8 and designed machines called bombes that built on earlier work by Polish codebreakers.
tossups.r: Those machines helped break the Enigma code. For 10 points, name this Bletchley Park codebreaker of World War II.

tossups.p: This man’s 1952 paper “The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis” [“mor-foh-JEN-uh-sis”] showed how chemicals that react and spread through tissue could form patterns like the spots and stripes on animals. Patterns of that kind are named for him.
tossups.r: Earlier, he imagined a machine that reads and writes symbols on an endless tape. For 10 points, name this British pioneer of computer science.

tossups.p: This man’s 1950 paper in the journal _Mind_ opens, “I propose to consider the question, ‘Can machines think?’” It predicted that by about the year 2000, an average judge would have no better than a 70 percent chance of spotting a computer after five minutes of questions.
tossups.r: That paper described the “imitation game,” a test later named for him. For 10 points, name this British computer scientist.

tossups.p: With David Champernowne [“CHAM-per-nown”], this man wrote an early chess program called Turochamp that no computer of the time could run. In 1952, he played a full game with it by working through its steps himself with pencil and paper.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician, the namesake of computer science’s top prize and of a test for machine intelligence.

tossups.p: At the National Physical Laboratory after World War II, this man designed the Automatic Computing Engine, or ACE, one of the first detailed plans for a computer that stores its programs in memory. He later wrote a programmers’ handbook for an early computer at the University of Manchester.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician, the namesake of a test of whether a machine can pass for a human.

tossups.p: The online puzzles called CAPTCHAs are named with an acronym that includes this man’s name, because they check whether a user is a human or a computer program. He suggested that instead of building an adult mind, scientists could build a “child machine” and teach it.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British computer pioneer who proposed a test in which a judge types questions to try to tell a human from a machine.

tossups.p: In 1952, this man was convicted under British laws that then made relationships between men a crime. Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologized for his treatment in 2009, and Queen Elizabeth II granted him a royal pardon in 2013.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this mathematician and World War II codebreaker, whose portrait was put on the Bank of England’s £50 note in 2021.

tossups.p: In July 1942, this man worked out a hand method for finding the wheel patterns of the German Lorenz cipher, nicknamed “Tunny.” Later that year, he traveled to the United States to work with U.S. Navy codebreakers, and at Bell Labs he met Claude Shannon.
tossups.r: He also helped break the Enigma code. For 10 points, name this British codebreaker who worked at Bletchley Park during World War II.

tossups.p: Andrew Hodges wrote a 1983 biography of this man subtitled _The Enigma_. Derek Jacobi played this man in _Breaking the Code_, Hugh Whitemore’s 1986 play based on that book.
tossups.r: Hodges’s book also inspired the 2014 film _The Imitation Game_, starring Benedict Cumberbatch. For 10 points, name this British mathematician and Bletchley Park codebreaker.

tossups.p: This man proved a version of the central limit theorem in his King’s College, Cambridge, fellowship dissertation, not knowing that Jarl Lindeberg had already proved it in 1922. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1951.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who described a “universal” machine that could carry out any other machine’s instructions.

tossups.p: Conway’s Game of Life and the redstone circuits in _Minecraft_ are both “complete” in a sense named for this man, meaning that, given enough time and memory, they can carry out any computation a computer can.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British pioneer of computer science, whose imaginary machine reads and writes symbols on a tape.

tossups.p: David Hilbert’s Entscheidungsproblem [“ent-SHY-doongs-pro-BLAYM”] asked for a method that could decide whether any statement in logic is provable. In a 1936 paper, this man showed that no such method exists, and he proved that no general method can decide whether any given program will eventually stop.
tossups.r: That paper was “On Computable Numbers.” For 10 points, name this British mathematician, whose imaginary machines became the basic model of what computers can do.

tossups.p: This man was appointed an OBE in 1946 for wartime work that stayed secret for decades. In 2021, the Bank of England put his portrait on its new £50 note, which entered circulation on his birthday, June 23.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this British mathematician who helped break Germany’s Enigma code at Bletchley Park during World War II.

tossups.p: This man described a “universal” machine that could imitate any other machine of its kind just by reading a coded description of it, an early version of the idea of a computer that stores its own programs. He introduced these machines in the 1936 paper “On Computable Numbers.”
tossups.r: He also proposed a famous test of machine intelligence. For 10 points, name this British mathematician whose imaginary computing machines are named for him.

trap.title: The man, not his machine
trap.body: Many things are named for Alan Turing: the Turing machine, the Turing test, the Turing Award, and “Turing complete” systems. A tossup about the man may mention them as “named for this man,” and players who just heard about the machine blurt out “Turing machine,” which is wrong. Others mix him up with John von Neumann, whose 1945 report described the stored-program computer, or with Charles Babbage, who designed mechanical computers in the 1800s.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this man,” “this mathematician,” or “this codebreaker,” say just “Turing” or “Alan Turing.” Babbage clues mention the Difference Engine, the Analytical Engine, and Ada Lovelace; von Neumann clues mention the Manhattan Project and game theory. Colossus, the Bletchley Park computer used against the Lorenz cipher, was built by Tommy Flowers, not Turing.
trap.line: Real answer line: Alan Turing (accept Turing; do not accept “Turing machine” or “Turing test”)
